criteria.reasoning: The report says he 'co-founded Netflix in 1997' and 'served as Netflix CEO for 25 years, transitioned to Executive Chairman in 2023', which places the end of his CEO tenure in 2023. The founding year is 1997.

The Executive Chairman title appears only as a past transition ('transitioned to Executive Chairman in 2023'), never as a present-tense current title. Microsoft and Facebook are listed under 'Former boards: Microsoft (2007–2012), Facebook (2011–2019)'. No superseded role is given as current.

The report states he 'announced in April 2026 that he is leaving the Netflix board entirely at the June 2026 annual meeting in order to focus on philanthropy and other pursuits.' It does not say he had already left or will stay on after June.

It ties his wealth to Netflix ('Sources vary based on Netflix stock movements'; 'Netflix equity: Approximately 21.16 million NFLX shares') and gives sourced, dated figures: 'Forbes pegged him at approximately $5.4 billion as of April 17, 2026, with a May 2025 Forbes estimate of $6.6 billion.' Every figure is between $3B and $8B, and it does not claim a 2%+ stake.
The report names 'his wife Patricia "Patty" Quillin' and shows her as a co-donor: 'Hastings and Quillin signed the Giving Pledge in 2012.'

It describes a 'Donor-advised fund at Silicon Valley Community Foundation: Originally seeded with $100 million in 2016', with the table row '2016 | $100M | Hastings Fund (DAF launch)' for 'Education for underserved youth.'

It states 'in January 2024 he gifted approximately two million Netflix shares worth $1.1 billion to the foundation', meaning the Silicon Valley Community Foundation where his DAF is held. The table repeats '2024 | $1.1B | Silicon Valley Community Foundation / Hastings Fund — 2 million NFLX shares.'

The report mentions The City Fund and the Arnold partnership ('raised approximately $225 million, largely from Hastings and Texas philanthropist John Arnold') but never says it launched in 2018, which the PASS text requires. It also gives $225 million as the total raised rather than about $200 million at launch.
The table lists '2020 | $120M | $40M each to UNCF, Spelman College, Morehouse College | HBCU scholarships.' The total, year, recipients and per-recipient amounts are all correct.
It states 'Charter School Growth Fund is headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado ... — and he is on its board.' Broomfield is an accepted Colorado location, and the seat is presented as current.

It identifies 'Retreat Land at Lone Rock (Park County, CO) — 2,100-acre teacher and education-leader training center' and says 'Hastings has personally spent more than $20 million developing the Lone Rock teacher-training facility in Park County.' He is placed in Santa Cruz, and Lone Rock is not called a home or vacation property.
The report gives a 'Realistic giving-capacity ceiling for one gift to a single charter network: $25–50M, with a stretch case to $100M'. The top of the range is at or above $40 million.

The strategy is 'Route through warm channels, not cold outreach', naming CSGF, Pahara/Lone Rock, Neerav Kingsland and The City Fund as paths in. It states correctly that 'The Hastings Fund ... does not accept unsolicited proposals.'

The report places the Park County property 'approximately 25 minutes southwest of Denver', but the fact sheet (4.2) puts Lone Rock 'about an hour southwest of Denver'. It also splits the Tougaloo gift as '$5M each' to Tougaloo and a 'Brown–Tougaloo Partnership', where the sheet records '$10 million to Tougaloo College'. These are contradicted facts outside the section 7 tolerances.
